title: Dynamic Typing and Duck Typing
description: Names, objects, and the philosophy that types should follow behavior

concepts.title: Names Bind to Objects, Not Variables
concepts.contentHtml:
Python's mental model is fundamentally different from C or Java. There are no variables in the C sense — boxes that hold values. There are only names bound to objects. Every value is an object on the heap; every name is a label that points to one.

When you write x = 5, you're not putting 5 into a box called x. You're creating an integer object 5 and binding the name x to it. y = x doesn't copy — it makes y point to the same object. This is why a = [1, 2]; b = a; b.append(3) mutates the list both names see — they're the same object.

Names live in namespaces (dictionaries, basically). Each function call creates a local namespace; the module has a global namespace; builtins is shared. The LEGB rule (Local, Enclosing, Global, Builtin) defines lookup order. Understanding this name/object split is the single biggest unlock in Python — most beginner confusion ("why did my list change?") traces back to it.

concepts.title: Duck Typing: If It Quacks Like a Duck
concepts.contentHtml:
Python doesn't care about an object's declared type — only about whether it supports the operations you perform on it. "If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck." A function that calls len(x) works on any object that defines __len__: list, string, dict, set, NumPy array, your custom class.

This is structural typing at runtime, in contrast to Java's nominal typing ("this object IS a List"). The benefits: massive code reuse, lightweight protocols, easy mocking in tests. The costs: errors only show up when you hit the offending line, not at compile time. Type errors that would be caught instantly in Java surface only after a function is actually invoked.

Modern Python adds type hints (PEP 484, 2014) that look like def add(x: int, y: int) -> int: return x + y. The runtime ignores them; tools like mypy, pyright, and pyre use them for static analysis. Hints are widely adopted in modern Python (FastAPI, Pydantic, large codebases) and bring back many compile-time guarantees without sacrificing duck typing's flexibility.

concepts.title: Mutable vs Immutable Default Arguments
concepts.contentHtml:
Python has a famous footgun: mutable default arguments. The default value of a parameter is evaluated once, when the function is defined — not on each call. So def add_item(item, items=[]): items.append(item); return items shares the same list across every call, accumulating items forever.

The fix: use None as the sentinel and create the mutable object inside: def add_item(item, items=None): items = items if items is not None else []; .... Every Python style guide warns about this; every Python developer has been bitten at least once.

The deeper insight: Python is full of small, sharp edges that follow logically from its model. Late binding closures (loop variables captured by reference, not value), the difference between is and ==, the way += on a list inside a tuple raises an exception and mutates the list. Each is consistent with the language design; each surprises beginners. Mastering Python is largely about internalizing these.

title: The Data Model and Dunder Methods
description: How everything in Python is a protocol, expressed via __methods__

concepts.title: Everything Is an Object
concepts.contentHtml:
In Python, everything is an object: integers, strings, functions, classes, modules, even types themselves. type(5) returns int; type(int) returns type; type(type) returns type (yes, type is its own type). This consistency is foundational.

Every object has an identity (id()), a type (type()), and a value. The identity never changes (it's the memory address in CPython). The type rarely changes. The value may or may not change — strings, tuples, frozensets, numbers are immutable; lists, dicts, sets, most user classes are mutable.

Functions are first-class objects: pass them as arguments, return them from other functions, store them in lists. This makes higher-order functions, decorators, and functional patterns natural. Classes are also objects — you can pass a class as a parameter, store it in a dict, even create one on the fly with type(name, bases, dict). This metaprogramming flexibility is part of what makes Python feel so expressive.

concepts.title: Dunder Methods: The Operator Protocols
concepts.contentHtml:
Python's operators are syntactic sugar over dunder (double-underscore) methods. a + b calls a.__add__(b); len(x) calls x.__len__(); x[5] calls x.__getitem__(5); x in container calls container.__contains__(x). Implementing the right dunder methods makes your custom class feel like a built-in.

Want your class to be iterable? Implement __iter__. Comparable? __eq__, __lt__. Used as a context manager? __enter__, __exit__. Hashable? __hash__. Stringifiable? __repr__ (for debugging) and __str__ (for display). Pickleable? __reduce__.

The unifying idea: the language defines protocols (collections of dunder methods); any class that implements a protocol participates in the corresponding language feature. There's no implements Iterable declaration like Java. Define __iter__, you're iterable. This is duck typing built into the core syntax.

concepts.title: Decorators and Context Managers
concepts.contentHtml:
A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a (usually modified) function. The @decorator syntax is sugar: @log\ndef f(): ... is identical to def f(): ...; f = log(f). Decorators show up everywhere: @property for managed attributes, @staticmethod, @functools.cache for memoization, framework decorators like @app.route.

A context manager is an object usable in a with block. The __enter__ method runs at block entry; __exit__ runs on exit (including exceptions). with open('f.txt') as f: opens a file, runs your code, closes the file even on exceptions. contextlib.contextmanager turns a generator function into a context manager via the yield statement, making them trivial to write.

Both decorators and context managers exemplify Python's higher-order spirit: pass code around as values, wrap behavior with hooks, compose features at the language level. Idiomatic Python uses both heavily.

title: Iterators, Generators, and Comprehensions
description: Lazy sequences, the iterator protocol, and pythonic data flow

concepts.title: The Iterator Protocol
concepts.contentHtml:
Anything with __iter__ is iterable. __iter__ returns an iterator — an object with __next__ that produces successive values, raising StopIteration when done. The for loop is sugar over this protocol: for x in xs: calls iter(xs) once, then next() until exhausted.

This protocol is everywhere. Lists, tuples, dicts, sets, strings, files, generators all implement it. enumerate, zip, map, filter, itertools functions all return iterators. Iterators are lazy: values are produced on demand, not all at once. open('huge.log') doesn't load the whole file — it reads line by line as you iterate.

One critical caveat: iterators are single-pass. Once consumed, they're done. list(iter([1,2,3])) works; calling list() on the same iterator again returns []. If you need to iterate multiple times, store in a list (eager) or define __iter__ to return a fresh iterator each call.

concepts.title: Generators: Functions That Pause
concepts.contentHtml:
A generator is a function with a yield statement. Calling it doesn't run the body; it returns a generator object. Each next() resumes execution until the next yield, returns that value, and pauses again. The function's local state is preserved between yields.

Generators are wildly powerful. They turn imperative code into lazy pipelines: def evens(): n = 0; while True: yield n; n += 2 is an infinite stream of even numbers, generated one at a time. Memory usage stays constant regardless of how many you consume.

Generator expressions are even more concise: (x*2 for x in big_list) creates a lazy generator, where [x*2 for x in big_list] creates an eager list. Same syntax, different memory profile. For pipelines processing millions of records, the generator version uses negligible memory; the list version may not fit in RAM. Idiomatic Python prefers generators when iterating once.
mathExpressions: \text{generator: function with yield} \implies \text{lazy iterator with preserved state}

concepts.title: Comprehensions: List, Dict, Set, Generator
concepts.contentHtml:
List comprehensions are Python's signature feature for transforming sequences: [expr for item in iterable if condition]. Equivalent to a map + filter but more readable and often faster because the bytecode is optimized.

The same syntax extends to dict comprehensions ({k: v for k, v in items}), set comprehensions ({x for x in xs}), and generator expressions ((x for x in xs)). The square brackets, curly braces, or parentheses determine the result type.

Comprehensions can be nested: [x for row in matrix for x in row] flattens a 2D list. They can include conditionals: [x if x > 0 else 0 for x in xs]. The Python style guide (PEP 8) suggests comprehensions for simple transformations and explicit loops when logic gets complex. The rule of thumb: if you need to break it across multiple lines or add a comment to understand it, switch to a regular loop.
mathExpressions: [f(x) \text{ for } x \in S \text{ if } P(x)] \equiv \{f(x) : x \in S,\, P(x)\}

title: The GIL, Async, and Concurrency
description: Why threads don't speed up CPU-bound code, and what to use instead

concepts.title: The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)
concepts.contentHtml:
CPython, the reference implementation, has a Global Interpreter Lock (GIL): a mutex ensuring only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time within a single process. The result: threads cannot speed up pure-Python CPU-bound code. You can have 100 threads on a 32-core machine and still use only one core for computation.

Why exists? CPython's reference counting (the primary garbage collector) isn't thread-safe without a global lock. Removing the GIL has been attempted many times; until 2024 each attempt either tanked single-thread performance or introduced subtle bugs. Python 3.13 introduced an experimental no-GIL build, and 3.14 made it officially supported, but it is still optional, not the default, and parts of the C extension ecosystem are still catching up.

What threads do help with: I/O-bound work. While one thread is waiting on a socket or disk, others run. The GIL releases during I/O. So a multithreaded web scraper can absolutely make many concurrent requests; a multithreaded image filter cannot speed up the actual filtering.
mathExpressions: \text{GIL: at most 1 thread executing Python bytecode at once} \implies \text{threads = no CPU parallelism}

concepts.title: asyncio and Cooperative Concurrency
concepts.contentHtml:
Python's modern concurrency story is asyncio: cooperative, single-threaded scheduling using async def and await. An async function returns a coroutine; await suspends until the awaited operation completes, freeing the event loop to run other tasks.

This avoids the GIL problem because there's just one thread. It excels at I/O-bound concurrency: web servers handling thousands of connections, scrapers fetching many URLs, database clients pipelining queries. Frameworks like FastAPI, Starlette, aiohttp, and async database drivers form a rich ecosystem.

The main gotcha: an async function is contagious. Calling it requires await, which requires an async context. Mixing sync and async code is awkward — the famous "function color" problem. Fully embracing async means rewriting much of your I/O layer. For new I/O-heavy services, asyncio is usually the right choice; for mixed or CPU-heavy work, threads or multiprocessing remain better fits.
mathExpressions: \text{async/await: cooperative scheduling on single thread, ideal for I/O concurrency}

concepts.title: Multiprocessing and Subinterpreters
concepts.contentHtml:
For CPU-bound parallelism, the workaround is multiprocessing: spawn separate Python processes, each with its own GIL. Communication uses pipes, queues, or shared memory. The multiprocessing module mirrors the threading API but works across processes.

The cost: process creation is expensive, and inter-process communication has serialization overhead (typically pickle). Sharing large objects between processes is painful. numpy and pandas sidestep this for numerical work because their hot loops run in C, releasing the GIL — multithreaded numpy actually does parallelize.

The future is interesting. Subinterpreters (a per-interpreter GIL since Python 3.12 via PEP 684, exposed as the concurrent.interpreters module in 3.14) give each interpreter its own GIL within a single process, with cheaper communication than multiprocessing. No-GIL builds (PEP 703) remove the GIL entirely. Mojo and Codon compile Python(-like) code to native code without the interpreter at all. Python's concurrency story is genuinely improving after decades of stagnation.
mathExpressions: \text{multiprocess: separate processes, separate GILs} \implies \text{true CPU parallelism}

title: The Ecosystem: pip, venv, NumPy, and Beyond
description: Packaging, dependencies, and Python's irreplaceable scientific stack

concepts.title: Packaging: pip, venv, and the New Wave
concepts.contentHtml:
Python packaging is famously messy. The basics: pip installs packages from PyPI; venv creates isolated environments per project so dependencies don't conflict. pip install -r requirements.txt in an activated venv has been the default workflow for years.

The classic pain points: managing transitive dependencies, reproducible installs, juggling Python versions across projects, and slow installs. The community has built better tools: poetry (lockfiles + dependency resolution), pipenv, conda (especially for scientific stacks with C dependencies), and pip-tools.

The current frontier is uv (Astral, 2024), which has absorbed the earlier rye project: a Rust-based replacement that is 10-100× faster than pip while handling the entire workflow (Python install, venv, dependency resolution, locking). The ecosystem is consolidating around these. If you're starting a new Python project in 2025+, uv is increasingly the default choice.

concepts.title: NumPy, Pandas, and the Scientific Stack
concepts.contentHtml:
Python's dominance in science and ML rests heavily on its scientific stack. NumPy provides n-dimensional arrays with vectorized operations implemented in C — operations on a million-element array run thousands of times faster than the equivalent Python loop. NumPy is the foundation under nearly all scientific Python.

Pandas builds on NumPy with labeled tables (DataFrame), pioneering a Python style of data wrangling. SciPy adds numerical algorithms; scikit-learn adds classical ML; matplotlib and seaborn add plotting; statsmodels adds statistics; SymPy adds symbolic math.

The ML revolution rides on this stack. PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX all expose Python APIs over high-performance C++/CUDA backends. Hugging Face transformers, spaCy, LangChain sit on top. The combination of Python's ergonomics with native-code performance via libraries is why Python — not Julia, not Lua — won ML.
mathExpressions: \text{Python ergonomics} + \text{C/CUDA performance via libraries} = \text{ML's lingua franca}

concepts.title: Web, Tooling, and Where Python Goes Next
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond science, Python has a strong web stack. Django (batteries-included, opinionated) and Flask (minimal, flexible) defined Python web for a decade. The modern era favors async-first frameworks: FastAPI (with Pydantic for type-validated APIs) is one of the fastest-growing web frameworks anywhere.

Tooling has matured rapidly. ruff (Astral) is a lint+format tool 10-100× faster than Python-based predecessors (flake8, pylint, black). mypy and pyright bring real static typing. pytest has displaced unittest as the dominant test framework. pre-commit hooks integrate them all.

The next era of Python is performance. Faster CPython (Mark Shannon's project) brings 10-50% speedups across releases. PyPy offers a JIT-compiled alternative interpreter, often 5-10× faster on long-running workloads. Mojo aims for full-stack Python+systems compilation. Python won't ever be C-fast, but it's catching up — and combined with the ecosystem advantage, that's enough to keep it the most popular language in the world.
